strengths: Well-motivated identification of system-hardware mismatch in existing MoE serving systems for edge devices, with clear empirical evidence (Figure 1 showing I/O stalls increasing from 38.5% to 80.1%)
Complete system design with principled integration of three complementary techniques: lossless compression, hierarchical caching, and cache-affinity scheduling
Theoretical contributions with provable guarantees: Theorem 3.1 (constant-factor approximation for scheduling) and Theorem 3.2 (maximum entropy cache planning)
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with significant performance improvements (up to 72.77% latency reduction, 6.76× throughput improvement) across multiple metrics and models
Security-aware approach addressing real vulnerabilities in quantized LLM inference, with timely motivation from recent adversarial attack literature
Careful systems implementation with zero-copy paradigm, memory coalescing, and OS-aware design considerations
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: each component (lossless compression, hierarchical caching, scheduling) is individually known; contribution primarily in their combination for a specific problem
Narrow experimental scope: evaluation limited to Jetson hardware only (not tested on Apple Silicon, Raspberry Pi, or mobile SoCs mentioned as targets); only 3 MoE models; synthetic workloads only
Loose theoretical approximation bound in Theorem 3.1 (3 - 1/L) shows minimal improvement with additional threads; no empirical validation against theoretical bound or lower-bound construction

Cache planning algorithm (Algorithm 4) relies on expensive grid search over configurations; computational complexity not analyzed; hyperparameter δ requires tuning; no comparison with simpler heuristics
Applicability limitations under-explored: encoder-decoder models show 4.99%-81.24% TPOT reduction vs 62.65%-97.97% for decoder-only; reasons for reduced effectiveness not thoroughly investigated
Statistical redundancy in BF16 exponent bits not deeply analyzed: unclear if phenomenon is fundamental or model-specific; limited to 3 models; unexplored for other precisions (FP32, FP8)

Resource interference claim of '7.47% peak SSD throughput reduction is negligible' may be too strong; no analysis of CPU power consumption or thermal implications; memory controller contention not fully quantified

Presentation issues: dense paper with notation introduced inconsistently; connection between rank-based workload modeling and actual expert identity mapping unclear; scheduling algorithm design choices (sort by pₙ₍ⱼ₎, choice of K shards) lack justification

Missing sensitivity analysis: no smooth performance curves varying memory budget; no ablation on sorting strategy or compression algorithm choice; cache planning robustness to workload statistics estimation errors unexplored
Reproducibility concerns: no code release mentioned; grid search hyperparameter δ not specified; procedure for obtaining rank-based expert activation patterns for new workloads unclear

strengths: Well-motivated identification of real mismatches between existing server-oriented MoE systems and edge device realities, with clear empirical evidence (Figure 1) of I/O dominance
Addresses important practical problem of on-device MoE inference while preserving exact model behavior without lossy quantization
Comprehensive system design integrating compression, hierarchical caching, and scheduling with attention to implementation details (zero-copy, memory coalescing)
Provides theoretical guarantees for scheduler (Theorem 3.1) and probabilistic modeling of cache planning (Theorem 3.2 on maximum entropy)
Solid empirical evaluation with realistic MoE models and workloads; ablation study demonstrates impact of design components
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty—primarily systems engineering combining off-the-shelf techniques (standard lossless compressors, hierarchical caching, I/O-computation overlapping). Better suited for systems venues (OSDI/SOSP) than ICML

Central claim of 'semantic losslessness' advantage is insufficiently substantiated. No empirical evidence that lossless compression prevents quantization-induced adversarial vulnerabilities (Shu et al. 2023) if model is later quantized or in full precision. Security benefits need formal analysis

Narrow experimental scope: only Jetson AGX Orin tested (despite mentioning Raspberry Pi and mobile phones); only 3 MoE models; missing comparisons with other compression strategies; no energy measurements; no released code limiting reproducibility

Weak theoretical guarantees: approximation ratio (3 - 1/L)·OPT approaches 3 for typical L values (6-12 threads → 2.83-2.92 approximation); simplifying assumptions (Poisson binomial modeling, known I/O delays, stationary expert activation) not validated

Insufficient analysis of cache planning: Algorithm 4 requires grid search with unclear hyperparameter selection (δ tolerance margin). Rank-based modeling assumes stationary expert distributions not validated across diverse prompts. Heuristic task partitioning lacks optimality justification

Missing important ablations and comparisons: no analysis of bit-field decomposition necessity vs. full-tensor compression; no direct compression technique comparison (ZSTD vs LZ4HC impact); baseline configurations potentially unfair (DeepSpeed coarse-grained memory control)

Experimental rigor issues: no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance; peak performance claims ('up to 72.77%') without discussing typical/representative scenarios; memory budget selection not justified

Questionable practical assumptions: Figure 4 I/O-decompression overlap assumes specific hardware characteristics not guaranteed on ARM-based edge CPUs; cache planning robustness to runtime OS memory reclamation not addressed; cold-start overhead not analyzed

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem identification with convincing diagnosis of system-hardware mismatch for edge MoE deployment (Figure 1 shows 38.5% to 80.1% I/O stall increase)
Sound information-theoretic foundation exploiting redundancy in BF16 exponent bits; ZSTD achieves 68% compression ratio approaching 66% Shannon entropy bound
Rigorous theoretical contributions with Theorem 3.1 providing (3-1/L) approximation ratio for scheduling and Theorem 3.2 proving maximum entropy cache pool planning
Comprehensive system co-design thoughtfully integrating lossless compression, hierarchical caching with multiple compression states, and cache-affinity scheduling
Strong empirical results with 62.65%-97.97% TPOT reduction and up to 6.76× throughput improvement; consistent across multiple models and baselines
Preserves exact model behavior (semantically lossless), addressing security vulnerabilities of quantization-based approaches
Well-designed evaluation with real-world workloads (ShareGPT), multiple state-of-the-art baselines, and informative ablation study demonstrating value of cache planning
Practical system implementation with attention to low-overhead details (zero-copy paradigm, memory-coalesced kernels, page cache awareness)
weaknesses: Limited hardware evaluation scope: only two Jetson AGX Orin variants tested despite claiming applicability to mobile phones and Raspberry Pi; no validation on these devices or other architectures like Apple Silicon

Reproducibility concerns: no code/artifacts provided, hyperparameters underspecified (grid search step size δ, tolerance margin τ), reliance on specific SSD model and OS-level page cache behavior limits portability

Inconsistent performance across model types: 62-98% improvement for decoder-only models vs. 4.99-81.24% for encoder-decoder models; large variance suggests limited generality without sufficient analysis of causes
Loose theoretical approximation ratio (3-1/L) without empirical analysis of practical tightness; gap between algorithm and optimal performance not characterized
Computational overhead of cache pool planning using grid search not reported; scalability to systems with many experts unclear
Insufficient analysis of approach limitations: when and why does it underperform? What if expert activation patterns change significantly? Sensitivity to compression ratio variations missing
Algorithm 1 (cache-affinity scheduling) is complex with multiple design choices; simpler alternative approaches not explored or compared
Cache planning heuristic (Algorithm 3) approximates scheduling without quantifying approximation error introduced; impact on final performance unclear

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies hardware-software mismatch between UMA edge platforms and existing MoE serving systems designed for discrete-memory servers, with concrete evidence (I/O stalls increase 2-5x)
Novel technical approach: first application of lossless compression to MoE inference, exploiting low-entropy BF16 exponent bits; clever hierarchical caching enables 2x coverage under same budget

Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 3.1 proves cache-affinity scheduler achieves (3-1/L)·OPT approximation; Theorem 3.2 proves cache planning produces maximum entropy distribution; proofs are rigorous and non-trivial

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple metrics (TPOT, TTFT, throughput), multiple models (decoder-only and encoder-decoder), multiple hardware/memory budgets, detailed ablations (76% gain from core system), sensitivity analysis showing robustness
Strong empirical results: 62-98% TPOT reduction, up to 42.49x throughput improvement, 3.03-42.49x end-to-end speedup on representative MoE models

Practical system engineering: thoughtful design choices (zero-copy paradigm, memory-coalesced kernels), honest page cache analysis (retains 66.7-74.4% gains without OS cache), ~10.6K LOC implementation
Clear problem motivation: excellent use of latency breakdowns, probability mass heatmaps, and compression ratio analysis to establish necessity and feasibility of approach
weaknesses: Limited generalizability: only evaluated on Jetson AGX Orin (UMA architecture); applicability to other edge devices (mobile phones, Raspberry Pi) claimed but unvalidated; future work mentions extending to heterogeneous memory systems
Narrow scope: only 3 MoE models tested (14-26B parameters); unclear if approach generalizes to different architectures or larger models; single hardware family evaluated

Theory-practice gap unexplained: approximation guarantee (3-1/L)·OPT with L=3 gives 2.67x, but empirical improvements are 3-42x; simplified makespan estimation in Algorithm 3 doesn't fully explain this gap

Missing key comparisons: no quantitative comparison with recent INT8/fine-grained quantization methods to validate 'lossless' advantage; FineMoE comparison relegated to appendix despite being recent baseline

Offline initialization cost underexplored: 6-20 minute compression time (Table 3) is non-trivial but barely discussed in main paper; memory overhead and practical deployment considerations need more analysis

Page cache dependency: while Table 2 shows robustness, baseline benefits from 66.7-74.4% of gains from OS page cache; this dependency on system state should be more prominent in main text rather than appendix

Incomplete sensitivity analysis: cache planning robustness tested only up to uniform distribution (α=1.0 in Table 4); extreme distribution changes not evaluated; no analysis of profiling error sensitivity

Presentation issues: Algorithm 1 complexity not well-motivated in main text; some critical engineering details (consolidating I/O with decompression) lack justification; abstract missing code URL despite availability claim

Limited experimental depth: no energy/power measurements; no scalability to multi-GPU edge deployments; no mobile device evaluation despite claiming applicability; batch size analysis limited to 1,4,16
